endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Establish an intake and monitoring process for thorough investigation of prospective solutions and mechanisms for incident detection, feedback, and follow-up.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: oversight and regulation of health care AI systems must be based on risk of harm and benefit accounting for a host of factors, including but not limited to: intended and reasonably expected use(s); evidence of safety, efficacy, and equity including addressing bias; AI system methods; level of automation; transparency; and, conditions of deployment.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: The AI team should develop policies and procedures on the review, implementation, and use of AI tools, ethical standards for AI use, safety and risk protocols, data use and privacy practices, and equitable use and access.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: The team should also identify any approval processes and evaluation criteria that would require updates/changes to the AI solution prior to pilot phase.

endorsements.title: Key decision points in adopting an AI solution
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership (Duke Health and partners)
endorsements.quote: Also includes guides for determining if AI products should be clinically integrated or abandoned.

endorsements.title: Scalable Agile Framework for Execution in AI for Medical AI Ethics Policy Design in Small- and Medium-Sized Enterprises
endorsements.quote: After completing the above, the decision-making stakeholders should come together as part of an existing review or showcase discussion to review the report, analyze the results, and come to a consensus on whether or not the work is "good enough" to proceed to deployment.

endorsements.title: Humanoid Colleagues and the Rheumatology Workforce: Preparing for a New Era
endorsements.quote: each stage is entered only through a gate of independently verified readiness criteria (Table 1 ).

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness in Emergency Medicine: Expert Consensus Opinion for Preparing the Workforce
endorsements.issuer: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
endorsements.quote: Each stage serves as a sequential gate; failure to meet criteria halts advancement until deficiencies are addressed and criteria are met, and culminates in a structured report to support transparent, accountable decision-making regarding AI adoption in emergency care.

commentary.bottom_line: Eight sources endorse a pre-deployment readiness gate with an evidence packet and no-go criteria, but no supplied study tests whether such a gate prevents unreviewed or unsafe activation. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and framework guidance alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests a readiness gate, and no study documents the hazard's frequency. The eight endorsements include two frameworks, two guidance documents, one descriptive framework, and three commentaries. Consensus across these sources shows agreement on the practice, but agreement among experts does not substitute for comparative evidence on outcomes.

The targeted failure is a tool that goes live without review or despite failed validation, bias, or unmitigable harm. No supplied study measures how often this happens or whether a gate with predefined no-go criteria stops such tools before they reach patients. The emergency medicine consensus describes halting advancement until criteria are met, which is a design claim that has not been tested.

Several sources describe sequential stage gates and a structured report for the decision makers. None of the supplied material reports how long a gate review takes, what staff time it consumes, or whether committees apply no-go criteria consistently in practice. Fidelity and burden therefore remain unmeasured.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare health systems or tool portfolios that use a formal readiness gate with those that do not. Useful outcomes include the share of tools stopped or revised before activation, post-deployment safety incidents, bias findings detected after go-live, and review time and staffing cost. Studies should also report inter-rater agreement on no-go decisions.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Several endorsements name equity and bias as review criteria, but whether gate packets capture subgroup performance for these populations, and whether safety-net systems have the resources to run such gates, has not been studied.
